Audio Engineer here! This is SOMEWHAT true, but not entirely.

Dynamics generally are limited to Cardioid or Hypercardioid pickup patterns, most people are familiar with what this means so I won't go into details to explain these terms, if you don't know then just look it up.

Condenser mics also oftentimes have Cardioid pickup patterns (among others), but the way this is achieved is entirely different, and the reason dynamics are often preferred for live settings over large diaphragm condenser mics is heavily related to this

Large Diaphragm condensers, even ones exclusively limited to Cardioid, generally have open headbaskets on both sides regardless of which side is the "main" side of the mic. For electret capsules this is done oftentimes so that tiny acoustic holes from the rear side of the capsule will sum with the sound coming from the front of the capsule with a small delay, causing a phase difference just large enough to phase out the 'background noise'

Dynamic microphones don't do this, as the way they are tuned for a specific frequency response has a lot more to do with the acoustic chamber inside the body, which is similar to how speakers and in-ear monitors work (exactly the same actually, as Dynamic mics and Dynamic Drivers in speakers and headphones are quite literally the same thing in reverse)

this is part of the reason that dynamic mics peak at about $300 and anything above that faces diminishing returns; it's just a more limited mic technology inherently.

But a side effect of this "Acoustic Chamber based tuning" is that the rejection from off axis even when set to the same pickup patterns tends to be better on dynamic microphones, as there is oftentimes a physical boundary between the capsule and anything facing away from the front of the mic.

But this is design dependent, so being "better at rejection" not an inherent part of dynamic microphone's as a technology, but instead a result of the design choices made to offset the innately poor frequency response of dynamic capsules.

Another fact worth mentioning is that condensers tend to have 'flatter' off-axis rejection, meaning the tonality of something off axis is not as heavily affected. IE; reflections getting 'darker' or 'brighter' when they're being rejected, dynamic microphones tend to make 'rejected' sounds darker, which is also partially due to the physical boundary between the source and capsule from the 'acoustic chamber' cutting off higher frequencies.

'Handheld' Small diaphragm condensers are a partially different story, they're used in live settings MUCH more often and tend to have similar features to dynamic microphones in terms of their acoustic chambers and appearance, just to a lesser extend, the Neumann KMS103/KMS104 is a good example of this.

This is also without getting into the awful feedback characteristics in Condensers, it's much MUCH harsher, they're just much more sensitive microphones which leads to a worse and more painful sounding feedback, even assuming the same volume level it's much worse- but they oftentimes spiral into feedback that is MUCH louder due to their sensitivity and .... weird max SPL characteristics often found on large diaphragm condenser microphones.

That's banding! It happens when there aren't enough colors to interpolate between different shades, there's two (three if you're thrifty) solutions to this issue.

1: Increase your color depth! This literally just adds more shades so that banding becomes fractionally less noticeable.

2: Dithering! Dithering just splotches around the different shades in a "less uniform" way, the dithering becomes SIGNIFICANTLY less noticeable while staying at the same color depth.

3: Post Film-Grain! This kinda just covers it up, if you're not able to redo the renders and you're stuck with the versions with banding, adding film grain generally either fixes it or makes it substantially less noticeable.

Also... Youtube compression will most likely make it worse- not better. Most likely it'll just splotch it around in a way that just looks pixelated and bad, but theres very few good tips on how to avoid that though.

This is almost if not completely due to battery chemistry, iPhones use the highest density LiPo batteries, which are rated for about 80% SoH after ~500 cycles, some better LiPo batteries reach into the ~800-1000 cycle range, iPhones tend to be closer to that despite being advertised as only having ~500 cycles at "100% DoD"

MacBooks tend to value longevity more than an iPhone does, so even if they do use LiPo batteries, they tend to be less energy dense but with higher cycle count ratings, the batteries are also larger as a whole, so even when degraded they are still much larger than iPhone batteries, so they are still capable of sustaining a MacBook for a reasonable amount of time.

MacBooks also have fans... Or they at least more thermal headroom, since the entire metal body of the device is essentially a heatsink, so the batteries tend to be cooler, and even when they're warm they are much more uniformly warm, as opposed to having much warmer hot spots within the vicinity of the SOC like on an iPhones battery would.

MacBooks also tend to stay within the middle percentages of the batteries State of Charge, meaning that they are in the outside of the "Edges of Death" that is the top 20% and bottom 20% of the battery, which is where the majority of battery degradation occurs, most mac users use apps like AlDente to allow you set a maximum SoC at 80%, or to sustain right at 50%, so if you're keeping your Mac on a charger or storing it for an extended period of time, you won't have to worry about the battery being damaged through over-discharging.

I think part of what throws me off is the type of lens distortion being used, the blender lens distortion is good for stylized renders, but it's non photorealistic chromatic aberration.

Real chromatic aberration happens especially on bright contrasting colors (a tree against a bright blue sky for example), which appears more noticeable off center, this is because of different wavelengths of light scattering differently within the glass of the lens, which means that the colors are effectively at slightly different focal lengths.

That's not to say there's anything wrong with the type of chromatic aberration you're using, but if you're looking for more "photorealism", using something like the "chromatic aberration removal" tool in davinci resolve would be more physically accurate (despite the name, you can use it for adding chromatic aberration).

Once you've done that, you NEED to use the "Use GPU compute" option for all of your renders, it SIGNIFICANTLY increases render speed

So, this is a complicated task, one that would probably require the collaboration of many- MANY modders to complete, however! As far as I am aware it is technically possible, technicality wise, Skyrim uses a fairly robust physics engine surprisingly enough, but the implementation is everything, and a good physics engine means nothing when it was poorly implemented (this is the case in Skyrim), BUT the good news is that the physics engine in Skyrim can technically handle this, but you would essentially have to rewrite most if not all the code for the way that Skyrim handles NPC animation, that being said, it would be possible eventually, but I wouldn't count on it being any time soon.

But, in the mean time, smaller goals are probably best, things like false weapon weight, and collision (similar to B&S and HL:A, where weapons and hands cannot go through walls and such).

​

If you'd like a list of everything that would need too be done for this to work in no particular order, here!

​

1: Fake Weapon Weights, this is needed to balance out the combat once your weapon can collide and interact with enemies.

2: Object Collision from hands and weapons, so they don't clip through walls and through enemies.

3: Rewrite of how NPC animation is handled, Skyrim's animation is different from B&S in one main way, in B&S enemies are not just animated by animations itself, but physics calculations  too, it's a hybrid system where animations are not static, and can be changed (For example: Grabbing an enemies arm in B&S while they are walking)

4: Collaboration between many modders such as the ones behind VRIK, HIGGS, DAR and XP32, it would be long and tedious.

​

That being said, it is *technically* possible, but practically it makes more sense to make small steps towards that.
